title: Rotate Image
statement: Rotate an `n × n` matrix by **90 degrees clockwise**, in place (without allocating a second matrix).

example.why: The first column, read from the bottom up (7, 4, 1), has become the first row.

idea: Moving every element straight to its rotated position needs careful four-way swaps. Two simple mirror operations give the same result.
**Transpose** the matrix: swap `matrix[i][j]` with `matrix[j][i]`, mirroring it across the main diagonal. Rows become columns.
Then **reverse every row**. Together: element `(i, j)` goes to `(j, i)` and then to `(j, n − 1 − i)` — exactly a clockwise quarter turn.

complexity.timeWhy: Every cell is touched a constant number of times.

steps.text: Our example: **`matrix = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
A 90° clockwise rotation = **transpose** (mirror across the diagonal from top-left to bottom-right), then **reverse each row**. Step 1: transpose.
Swap (0, 1) with its mirror cell (1, 0): 2 and 4 trade places.
Swap (0, 2) with its mirror cell (2, 0): 3 and 7 trade places.
Swap (1, 2) with its mirror cell (2, 1): 6 and 8 trade places.
The matrix is transposed: its rows have become its columns. Step 2: reverse each row. Row 0: [1, 4, 7] → **[7, 4, 1]**.
Done. The matrix is rotated 90° clockwise: `[[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]`. It was changed in place, so nothing is returned.
